episode.episode: Philips Hue: The smart home’s light bulb moment
episode.showDescription: Version History is a show about the best gadgets ever. And the worst ones. And the ones that might have changed the world, if they ever actually shipped. Every week, your favorite people from The Verge and beyond hang out to tell and debate the story of a gadget, app, website, or any other tech product, and try to determine the item’s true legacy. Because not every product is a hit, but every product has a story. And the ones that really matter aren’t always the ones you think. From the Verge and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
episode.episodeDescription: The humble light bulb might be the ultimate success story in the smart home. Our connected, adaptable homes are supposed to be customizable, connected to everything, and incredibly easy to use, and nothing has made that work quite like Philips Hue lights. In this episode, The Verge's David Pierce and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy are joined by smart home journalist and expert Richard Gunther to tell the Hue's story. We trace the product's history from its origins in the smartphone revolution, try to figure out how Philips managed to turn a staggeringly expensive lightbulb into a must-have gadget, and look at whether there's even more invention left in the future of lighting. We’re also on video! Check us out on YouTube. Subscribe to The Verge for unlimited access to theverge.com, subscriber-exclusive newsletters, and our ad-free podcast feed. We love hearing from you! Email your questions and thoughts to vergecast@theverge.com or call us at 866-VERGE11. Learn more about your ad choices. Visit podcastchoices.com/adchoices

transcript_window.text: And this is going to immediately divert us from the history here.

This is the thing I've been thinking a lot about because, like you described, Jen, they started, George Yanni's team in particular, and George becomes kind of the driving force of the whole Hue project.
But at the beginning, they were setting out to use the iPhone basically as a way to really quickly prototype interfaces that they were planning to eventually make into hardware remotes.

The idea was like instead of having to make new physical prototypes every time we want to try something or move a button, we can just do it on a screen, get a feel, and then only make hardware ones for further along.
But then in the course of doing this, they decide, oh, this is actually a software problem.
and we should just go back to making things on the phone and let the phone be the primary interface to a lot of this stuff.

And the thing I found myself wondering over and over is there's an alternate universe here where instead what this group of people does is go and make a bunch of really interesting new ideas about remotes and maybe like cast it far enough along and we end up at like, can we reinvent the light switch?
But instead this becomes pretty quickly a purely software enterprise.
And what I wanna know is, are either of you as bummed as I am what it might look like to reinvent the light switch.
Richard, what do you think?
Should we have done this?
I think that's an amazing idea.
A number of companies have tried to do this, I would argue, largely unsuccessfully.
Every time somebody tries to come up with a creative new spin on the light switch, I just kind of wince a little bit.

There's a bunch of folks in this space who refer to poorly designed light switches as Gunther switches, I have such an issue with poorly ergonomically designed light Don't going on the GE Sync switches.
Oh.
This is a great thing to be known for.
People being mad at their light switches, associating them with you, I think is what a great legacy that And after me.
Yeah.
It's an honor.
For sure.
No, I would have loved that.
And, I mean, you could argue that Sonos sort of went down that same path, creating their own remotes for their system, up just reverting back to the phone.
Yeah, that's very true.
We all did converge back there, right or wrong.
That's where we landed.
